subject: Anatomy
summary: The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles and tendons that stabilize the shoulder joint and enable arm elevation. Understanding its anatomy helps diagnose common shoulder pain and guide management.

sections.p: The rotator cuff consists of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis, forming a cuff around the humeral head.
All four tendons insert on the proximal humerus: supraspinatus on the greater tubercle, infraspinatus and teres minor on the posterior facet, subscapularis on the lesser tubercle.
b: Infraspinatus lies posterior to the scapular spine

sections.p: The cuff lies deep to the subacromial bursa and is bordered anteriorly by the coracoid process and posteriorly by the scapular spine.
Arterial supply comes from the suprascapular artery (supraspinatus, infraspinatus) and the circumflex humeral arteries (subscapularis, teres minor).
b: Vascularity is poorest at the supraspinatus insertion
Poor blood flow predisposes to tendon degeneration

sections.p: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor receive innervation from the suprascapular nerve; subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.
b: Nerve injury can mimic tendon tears

sections.p: Collectively the cuff stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid and initiates arm elevation: supraspinatus starts abduction, infraspinatus/teres minor externally rotate, subscapularis internally rotates.
b: Prevents superior migration of humeral head

sections.p: Rotator cuff pathology ranges from tendinopathy to full‑thickness tears, often due to impingement, overuse, or trauma. In low‑resource settings, infections (TB, HIV‑related myositis) and chronic hemoglobinopathies can weaken tendons.
b: Impingement syndrome: pain on overhead motion

t.b: Detects tendon integrity when MRI unavailable; shows partial vs full‑thickness tear
Gold standard for tear size, retraction, muscle atrophy; guides surgical planning
Assesses acromial morphology and humeral head position; may reveal osteophytes causing impingement

sections.p: Key physical signs include painful arc (60‑120°), positive Jobe’s (supraspinatus) test, and external rotation lag sign (infraspinatus/teres minor).
b: Weakness on resisted abduction points to supraspinatus tear

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of shoulder function after trauma
Severe, unrelenting shoulder pain with fever (possible septic bursitis)
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting massive cuff tear

faq.q: Why is the supraspinatus most often torn?
faq.a: It has the smallest blood supply and passes under the acromion, making it vulnerable to impingement and degeneration.

faq.q: Can a rotator cuff tear heal without surgery?
faq.a: Small partial tears may improve with physiotherapy and activity modification; large or full‑thickness tears often need surgical repair.

faq.q: How does HIV affect the rotator cuff?
faq.a: Chronic HIV can cause myopathy and tendon degeneration, increasing risk of spontaneous tears.

exam: Describe the four rotator cuff muscles, their insertions, and primary actions.
Explain how supraspinatus impingement produces a painful arc and which imaging modality confirms a tear.
Outline the initial management steps for a patient with suspected rotator cuff tendonitis in a low‑resource setting.
